caption:
Skyfall AI says its AI CEO, Steve, now runs three real online businesses with a team of AI agents.
One grew monthly revenue 2.3x in a quarter, the company says. Another stopped a five year decline.
The owner still sets the rules, and Skyfall is putting $2 million into buying 5 more startups for Steve to run.

Would you work for a company run by an AI CEO?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: Skyfall AI, a San Francisco startup, announced on November 9, 2026 a system called Steve that it describes as the first AI CEO. According to the company's press release, Steve is an autonomous business harness built to run digital businesses such as SaaS products and Shopify apps, and it is already running three businesses that Skyfall acquired.

Skyfall says Steve coordinates a team of specialist AI agents and relies on what it calls a code world model: an executable model built from a company's records and inputs that simulates possible actions and forecasts their effects. Each proposal comes with a forecast, a time frame and a confidence level. When real results differ from the forecast, Steve updates its model and plans, the company said.

The release also describes a form of self-improvement in which Steve changes its own code, skills, agent setup, tests and world model, linking each change to the problem that prompted it. In one example, growth and engineering agents kept handing a website deployment back and forth because one of them lacked access. Skyfall said Steve changed its harness so that the orchestrating agent settles such conflicts.

Skyfall reported early numbers for two of the three businesses. The first has run on Steve for more than two months, and the company says its total monthly revenue grew 2.3 times over the last quarter. The second had five years of steady revenue decline, high churn and a stretch with no new paying users; Skyfall says its revenue has stabilized and it is gaining customers again. The third business was added one week before the announcement, and the company said it is too early to report results. None of these figures has been independently verified, and the businesses are not named.

Skyfall says owners keep control through a policy engine. Decisions are checked against ordered rules covering the type of decision, spending and customer impact, and each one can run automatically, run with a notification, wait for approval or be blocked. As an example, the company said an owner could allow automatic refunds up to $30 and require approval for larger ones. Skyfall also said it plans public dashboards that show each business's goals, metrics, decisions and harness changes under anonymous names.

Alongside the launch, Skyfall committed $2 million to acquire five early stage startups that will run entirely on Steve, and invited founders to apply. The plan extends an idea the company described in July, when it said it would buy a small software or e-commerce business for up to $1 million and try to double its revenue within six months, as reported by Gizmodo and BetaKit.

The company was founded by Sam Pasupalak, Sumit Pasupalak and Kaheer Suleman. Sam Pasupalak and Suleman previously co-founded Maluuba, a deep learning lab that Microsoft acquired in 2017. Skyfall has offices in San Francisco and Toronto, and its press release lists Fidelity, Touring Capital, M13 and Inovia Capital as backers.

Skyfall is making a concrete claim with real revenue attached, but the evidence is still the company's own reporting on unnamed businesses, and one of the two results is a stabilization rather than growth. The approval rules suggest that, for now, humans still decide where the money goes on anything large.
The public dashboards Skyfall promised will be the first chance for outsiders to check whether the revenue claims hold up over several more months.
